extracted.intended_audience: general readers researching the 'Bad Art Friend' controversy; journalists and students of media ethics
extracted.subtask_short: Wikipedia article on viral NYT feature
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic summary of the 2021 New York Times Magazine feature 'Who Is the Bad Art Friend?' and the ensuing legal, ethical, and cultural fallout. Covers background, writing process, reception, related coverage, and institutional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-judgmental, balanced reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "a non-judgmental account of a complex dispute"; "a story that would present both Ms. Dorland's and Ms. Larson's side faithfully, while explaining to readers how, moment by moment, all of this unfolded."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kolker pitched and reported the piece intending to present both sides fairly; he worked to establish "trust and understanding" with both subjects, including off-the-record interviews, before beginning work. Use of this approach suggests standards of balance, careful chronology, and subject engagement in longform reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid flattening complex stories into binaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that the debate "risks flattening the piece into a tale of good guys and bad guys."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters and readers should be wary of simplifying complex interpersonal and ethical disputes into moral binaries; maintain nuance and resist emotionally driven partisanship that obscures context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh public interest against harm to subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Question raised whether publication was "really worth the damage that they've done to these two women's lives?" and critical commentary that the journalist may be the primary beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic decisions should consider potential harms to individuals and communities alongside public interest and newsworthiness; editorial teams may need to evaluate trade-offs before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair use / transformative-use analysis in alleged appropriation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of whether what was called plagiarism was really "fair use"; court and commentators referenced transformative use and divergent creative motivations as weighing in favor of fair use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments hinge on factors like purpose and character (transformative purpose), nature of the copied material, amount/substantiality, and effect on market; side-by-side comparisons of source and work and consideration of differing artistic motivations are relevant. The page notes a later ruling finding Larson's story protected by fair use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism vs ownership of life story / protection of expressive language
rubrics_metrics.description: Dorland "concedes she does not own her life story. Rather, she claims ownership of the unique way she conveyed her thoughts and feelings..." and Larson admitting "it literally has sentences that I verbatim grabbed from Dawn's letter on FB."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish unprotectable facts or events (life experiences) from protectable, original expressive phrasing; verbatim copying of distinctive expressive language can give rise to plagiarism/copyright concerns even when underlying facts are shared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction craft: characterization and prose quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical assessments of the short story: The New Yorker said it "makes a cartoon of the donor character," "the prose is bad," and "over-relies on identity-inflected hand-waving."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations of fiction should consider depth and nuance of characterization, quality of prose, and whether identity markers are used as shallow explanatory devices rather than fully developed motives or characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational accountability and internal review
rubrics_metrics.description: GrubStreet announced it would "hire an expert to look into the ongoing dispute," launched an internal review after release of potentially disparaging emails, and some leaders left their positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When controversies implicate institutional values, organizations may need transparent reviews, independent expertise, and personnel/accountability measures. Release of internal communications can prompt reputational and governance responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop etiquette and consent when using others' material
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence in which a draft story shared with a writing group was recognized as resembling a real participant; author changed a character name but "had trouble modifying the text of a letter" and declined to let the real person read the story when asked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When fiction is inspired by real people or workshop material, best practices include seeking consent, sufficiently altering identifying details and phrasing, and respecting workshop norms to avoid personal and legal conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public discourse dynamics and social-media effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece "went viral" and prompted intense online debate where readers "identified emotionally with one side—and got mad," producing descriptions like the "internet's kangaroo court."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Viral coverage can amplify polarization, simplify narratives, and cause collateral harm; writers and editors should anticipate online dynamics and consider mitigations (context, clarifications, follow-ups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal outcomes: copyright and defamation resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Note that on September 14, 2023 the U.S. District Court ruled Larson's story was protected by fair use and that Larson was not defamed by Dorland.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal rulings can resolve disputes differently across claims (copyright vs defamation). Reporting and evaluation should track judicial outcomes and understand that court standards (e.g., fair use factors, defamation elements) ultimately determine liability.
